title: UI Kits, Design Tokens, and Reusable Components
description: Build a small and consistent component system with clear APIs, semantic tokens, documented variants, and accessibility built into shared primitives.
learningOutcomes: Distinguish design systems, component libraries, and one-off page styles.
Define semantic tokens for repeated colors, spacing, typography, and control dimensions.
Create reusable components with explicit types, variants, and states.
Choose composition rather than a sprawling set of boolean props.
Build accessibility requirements into shared buttons, fields, and alerts.
Document a small UI kit and refactor feature screens to consume it.
Build accessible fields and choose a ref pattern for the installed React version.

blocks.text: A design system makes decisions reusable

A design system combines principles, visual tokens, component contracts, usage guidance, and a way to evolve them consistently. A component library supplies reusable implementation; tokens name repeated visual decisions; documentation describes which component to choose and how to use it. The goal is consistent behavior and faster change—not abstraction for its own sake.
Name visual choices with semantic tokens

A raw color or spacing value becomes difficult to maintain when repeated across many files. A semantic token describes why a value exists, such as --color-action-primary or --space-control. This allows a theme update to change the shared decision in one place. A useful token describes a role rather than one page, temporary feature, or incidental pixel value.

blocks.caption: Semantic tokens using CSS custom properties

blocks.text: A component needs a clear public contract

A component API should expose the choices consumers need while hiding incidental implementation details. A Button might support primary, secondary, and danger variants plus disabled/loading states, but should still render a real button. TypeScript can restrict supported choices, and examples/documentation explain visual and interaction behavior. Avoid adding many options before a repeated use case justifies them.

steps.title: Limit the documented variants
steps.explanation: The variant union allows only supported values. The state props describe behavior rather than exposing arbitrary styling controls.

steps.title: Use defaults to keep common use simple
steps.explanation: The primary variant is the default, while callers may choose another supported variant or state.

steps.title: Preserve native button behavior
steps.explanation: A native button provides keyboard and activation semantics. Disable it while unavailable; the app can add suitable status announcements when the loading context needs them.

blocks.text: Prefer composition to many interacting flags

A component gets hard to understand when it has dozens of unrelated props such as compact, withIcon, bordered, showHeader, hideFooter, and many combinations. Passing children or composing small subcomponents often creates a simpler API. Reuse a stable behavior or visual pattern, while keeping page-specific business rules in the feature that owns them.
Accessibility belongs in the shared contract

A reusable field should support a programmatic label, help text, invalid state, associated error message, visible focus, and disabled/required semantics. Buttons need clear accessible names, keyboard behavior, and enough contrast across variants. An alert should communicate urgency appropriate to the message. When these rules live in the shared primitive, each page is less likely to implement them differently or forget an important state.

blocks.title: A UI kit should not become a second application
blocks.text: Keep low-level primitives independent from feature-specific business logic. Higher-level patterns such as LessonCard or SearchForm may compose the primitives in a feature folder. Provide sensible defaults and documented extension points; do not make every one-off layout decision a new token or universal prop.

blocks.prompt: What is the main benefit of a semantic token such as --color-action-primary?

options.text: It names the purpose of a visual choice so many components can change consistently
options.feedback: Semantic tokens capture intent and centralize a repeated visual decision.

options.text: It automatically guarantees enough contrast everywhere
options.feedback: Tokens centralize values, but contrast still depends on the foreground/background pair and context.
A token does not explain a component's behavior or usage.

options.text: It forces all pages to share one layout
options.feedback: Tokens coordinate visual decisions but do not require identical page composition.

blocks.explanation: Use tokens to express intent and manage repeated choices consistently.

blocks.prompt: A reusable React button should normally be implemented as a clickable div so any style can be applied.

options.feedback: A div does not automatically provide button semantics, keyboard activation, or disabled behavior.
A native button already provides expected interaction semantics and can be styled.

blocks.explanation: Prefer the native semantic element that fits the interaction.

blocks.prompt: Which practices are useful in a shared UI kit? Select all that apply.

options.feedback: A clear contract lets consumers understand supported use.

options.text: Include keyboard and accessibility behavior in primitives
options.feedback: Shared behavior makes accessibility more consistent across screens.

options.text: Add every possible prop before real use cases appear
options.feedback: Premature abstraction increases the number of combinations consumers must understand.

options.text: Keep feature-specific business rules out of low-level primitives
options.feedback: This keeps the primitive reusable and less coupled to a specific feature.

blocks.explanation: Good design systems balance consistent defaults with small, understandable component contracts.

blocks.title: Create and document a small UI kit
blocks.context: Implement the components in your running React project. The lesson editor saves drafts but does not compile TSX.
instructions: Define semantic CSS tokens for text, surface, primary action, control spacing, and radius.
Create a Button with primary, secondary, and danger variants.
Support disabled/loading while preserving native button behavior.
Create a TextField with label, help text, invalid state, and a linked error message.
Create an Alert with semantics appropriate to the urgency of its message.
Document variants, states, and accessibility behavior in a README section.
Refactor two existing screens to use the shared components without changing behavior.
Verify keyboard focus, contrast, disabled behavior, and narrow viewport layout.
requirements: Repeated visual values are centralized with semantic tokens where appropriate.
The component APIs are explicitly typed with sensible defaults.
Native semantic HTML and keyboard behavior are preserved.
Field labels and error descriptions are programmatically associated.
The primitive layer has no feature-specific business logic.
The documentation describes supported variants, states, and accessibility expectations.
hints: Start with the component choices a real consumer needs; add variants only when a pattern repeats.
Use htmlFor/id and aria-describedby to connect labels, help text, and errors.
Create tokens for decisions shared by several primitives, not for every one-off pixel value.
successCriteria: Two feature screens can use the same Button API.

items: A design system combines reusable decisions, tokens, component contracts, patterns, and documentation.
Semantic tokens describe why a value exists and make shared changes easier.
Component APIs should be explicit, typed, and intentionally small.
Prefer composition and native semantic HTML to many boolean flags or clickable divs.
Include keyboard, focus, disabled, error, and contrast requirements in shared components.

blocks.text: Build a field with an accessible error contract

A reusable field should connect its label, helper text, invalid state, and error message. Use `htmlFor`/`id`, `aria-invalid`, and `aria-describedby` so meaning is not conveyed by color alone. Keep keyboard focus visible with `:focus-visible`; do not remove the browser outline without an equally visible replacement.

steps.title: Define the field contract
steps.explanation: The API names the label, value, change handler, help text, and optional error.

steps.title: Create description IDs
steps.explanation: The input references helper/error text rendered for this instance. IDs should be unique, and `aria-describedby` should only list rendered IDs.

steps.title: Connect label and error semantics
steps.explanation: `htmlFor` connects label and input; `aria-invalid` exposes the invalid state and `aria-describedby` connects descriptions. Error meaning must not rely on color alone.

steps.title: Keep focus visible
steps.explanation: The code comments show a clear `:focus-visible` ring. Never suppress the outline unless an equally visible focus indicator replaces it.

blocks.text: Advanced component patterns are contracts, not badges

items: Compound components such as `Card.Header`, `Card.Body`, and `Card.Footer` can express shared structure with flexible children; use them when composition improves the consumer API.

In React 18 and earlier, `forwardRef` can expose a DOM node for focus, measurement, or library integration. React 19 lets function components receive `ref` as a prop; match the pattern to the installed version.

A polymorphic `as` prop changes the rendered element and valid attributes/ref types. Add it only when real consumers need it; preserve link-versus-button semantics and avoid generic typing complexity without a use case.
Loading/disabled feedback and visible focus belong in the shared component contract. Loading icons should not create duplicate accessible names.
Atomic Design (atoms/molecules/organisms/pages) is one organizing vocabulary, not a required folder hierarchy.

blocks.prompt: The project uses React 18. A parent form needs to focus the native input inside a reusable custom field. Which guidance is correct?

options.text: Expose the DOM node with `forwardRef` when needed and preserve accessible label/error relationships
options.feedback: In React 18 and earlier, `forwardRef` is the standard pattern when a function component needs to receive and forward a ref.

options.text: Add `role="textbox"` to a div and pass a ref without forwarding it
options.feedback: A role does not create native input behavior or forward the ref to the actual DOM node.

options.text: Use `forwardRef` for every component whether consumers need a ref or not
options.feedback: Expose refs when consumers have a real focus, measurement or integration need; extra API surface has maintenance cost.

options.text: Ignore the React version because `forwardRef` is required in every version
options.feedback: React 19 allows `ref` as a prop for function components, so the pattern is version-sensitive.

blocks.explanation: React 18 and earlier use `forwardRef` when ref forwarding is needed; React 19 supports `ref` as a prop for function components. Preserve semantic controls and accessible descriptions in either version.

blocks.text: Deep dive: tokens, component contracts, and accessible variants

A design system is a set of decisions that should remain consistent as the product grows: tokens name visual values, components encode repeated behavior, and usage guidance explains which component belongs to which job. A reusable component needs a constrained public API. A prop such as `variant: string` admits misspellings and unknown values; a union limits the contract. Avoid a single 'god component' with many unrelated boolean props.

steps.title: Restrict public choices with union types
steps.explanation: The supported variants and sizes are explicit, and consumers cannot pass arbitrary misspelled strings without a type error.

steps.title: Encode behavior, not only visuals
steps.explanation: Disabled and loading have meaningful behavior. A loading action cannot be submitted repeatedly, and aria-busy can communicate the pending state to assistive technology.

steps.title: Keep semantic HTML and a small API
steps.explanation: A native button supplies keyboard behavior and activation semantics. Prefer a clear variant/size contract over unrelated props that change the component into multiple hidden components.

items: Tokens centralize color, spacing, type scale, radii and elevation so themes and global tuning do not require editing every component.
Variants should describe a small, intentional set of semantic choices (`primary`, `danger`), not arbitrary style strings that let each caller invent new design language.
Use native button/link semantics; icon-only controls need an accessible name, disabled/loading states need visible feedback, and focus indicators must remain visible.
Composition often scales better than a component with many unrelated boolean props; use slots or subcomponents when the structure itself is meaningful.
Adopting MUI or another library is a product trade-off: consider accessibility, theming, bundle impact, version churn, customization cost and the team's existing patterns.

blocks.prompt: Why is `variant: 'primary' | 'secondary' | 'danger'` a better component contract than `variant: string`?

options.text: It guarantees the component can never render incorrectly at runtime
options.feedback: Types catch many authoring mistakes at compile time, but runtime values and visual/accessibility bugs still need testing.

options.text: It documents and constrains the supported variants, catching misspellings during type checking
options.feedback: A finite union makes the public API explicit and allows the compiler to reject unsupported variants.
The component still needs styling rules for each supported variant.
Theme support comes from design tokens and theme architecture, not the variant type alone.

blocks.explanation: A component's type is part of its API and should constrain choices rather than accepting any string.

blocks.title: Design a Button API and a token set
blocks.context: Create a small reusable component contract that handles visual variants and interaction/accessibility consistently.
instructions: Define design tokens for brand, danger, spacing and radii instead of duplicating values.
Create a ButtonVariant union and a ButtonSize union.
Implement disabled and loading behavior with a native button element.
Add a visible focus state and an accessible name for icon-only usage.
Write usage examples and explain when a link should be used instead of a button.
Implement a TextField with label/help/error association via `aria-describedby`, `aria-invalid`, and visible `:focus-visible` styling.
requirements: Component props restrict variants and sizes to supported values.
Design values are named tokens rather than repeated unexplained literals.
Disabled/loading states prevent inappropriate repeated actions and communicate status.
Keyboard focus remains visible and controls have accessible names.
Navigation is represented with a link; an in-page action is represented with a button.
A field's label, helper text and error are programmatically associated; keyboard focus remains visible.
hints: A union catches misspellings that string does not.
Choose a semantic native control first, then add visual variants.
Token names express a role (`color-danger`) rather than an isolated hex value.
successCriteria: Invalid variant/size values fail type checking.
The component has sensible defaults and a small API.
Tokens are centrally named and reused.
The usage explanation distinguishes navigation from actions.
A screen reader can discover the label and error description, and keyboard users can see focus.

items: Tokens preserve design consistency; component contracts preserve consistent behavior.
Constrain variants and prefer composition over many unrelated boolean props.
Accessibility and semantics are part of the component API, not optional polish added at the end.
